castelo.name: Guimarães Castle
castelo.short: A 10th-century castle on a granite hill: the “cradle of Portugal” and one of the country’s Seven Wonders
castelo.long: Countess Mumadona Dias founded the castle around 958 to shield her monastery from Moorish and Norse raids. In the late 11th century Count Henry of Burgundy rebuilt it as his residence; tradition says Afonso Henriques, the first King of Portugal, was born here. The shield-shaped walls with battlemented towers and the central keep come from a Gothic remodelling in the 13th century and the restoration of 1937–1940. The castle is open to visitors, and the wall-walk looks out over the whole city.
castelo.history:
In the mid-10th century the settlement of Vimaranes lived under threat: Moors raided from the south, Norsemen from the sea. Countess Mumadona Dias, widow of Count Hermenegildo Gonçalves, founded a monastery on the low ground and ordered a castle of refuge on the top of Monte Largo. A deed of 958 already names the fortress as the Castle of São Mamede. It was probably no more than a tower inside a palisade.

At the end of the 11th century King Alfonso VI of León gave the lands of the County of Portucale to Henry of Burgundy. Count Henry and his wife Teresa made Guimarães their residence. They pulled down the old work, raised the keep and enlarged the enclosure with two gates: the main gate to the west and the “Traitor’s Gate” to the east. Tradition says their son Afonso Henriques was born here. In 1127 he held out inside these walls against Alfonso VII, and on 24 June 1128 he defeated his mother’s army on the neighbouring field of São Mamede. That battle is counted as the birth of Portugal.

The castle took its present form under King Dinis around 1300: a shield-shaped plan, battlemented towers and a wall-walk. It was besieged again in 1322, 1369 and 1385. In 1389 John I merged the upper and lower towns into a single town of Guimarães; its wall then ran for two kilometres with eight towers and eight gates.

From the 15th century artillery made the castle useless. The town jail moved in during the 16th century, a royal hay store in the 17th. In 1836 the town council came within one vote of demolishing it for paving stone. In 1881 it became the first building in the Minho listed as a historic monument of the first class, and in 1908–1910 a National Monument. It was restored in 1937–1940 for Portugal’s 800th anniversary and reopened on 4 June 1940. In 2007 it was voted one of the Seven Wonders of Portugal; in 2022 it received 302,761 visitors.
facts: A deed of 958 already names the castle as São Mamede.
Tradition says Afonso Henriques, the first King of Portugal, was born here.
The Battle of São Mamede was fought below the walls on 24 June 1128.
In 1836 a proposal to demolish the castle for paving stone failed by one vote.
A National Monument since 1910 and one of the Seven Wonders of Portugal since 2007.
castelo.tip: The castle opens daily from 10:00 to 18:00, last entry 17:30. A ticket costs €5, or €8 combined with the Dukes’ Palace. The keep is closed, but the wall-walk takes you all the way round. Between the castle and the palace stands the Romanesque church of São Miguel, and the statue of Afonso Henriques stands by the palace ramp. Closed on 1 January, Easter Sunday, 1 May, 24 June and 25 December.
